Q38789.title: Battle of Stalingrad
paras: The Battle of Stalingrad, from August 1942 to February 1943, was fought between Nazi Germany and its allies, chiefly Romania, Italy and Hungary, and the Soviet Union for the city of Stalingrad on the Volga. It is considered the largest and deadliest urban battle in history and the deadliest battle of the Second World War, and the Soviet victory is generally seen as the turning point of the war in Europe.

In the summer of 1942 Germany struck south rather than at Moscow. Stalingrad was an industrial city making artillery, and the Volga a vital shipping route; Hitler also prized the city for bearing Stalin's name and added it to the campaign's objectives in July. On 23 August Friedrich Paulus's 6th Army and part of the 4th Panzer Army attacked, while Luftwaffe raids reduced much of the city to rubble; its civilians had not been evacuated, and tens of thousands were killed. Stalin's Order No. 227, 'Not a step back!', forbade retreat.

From 13 September the fighting moved into the city itself. Vasily Chuikov's 62nd Army, down to about 20,000 men, held a narrowing strip along the river. The hill of Mamayev Kurgan, the central railway station and the grain elevator changed hands again and again, snipers fought from the rooftops, and Sergeant Yakov Pavlov's platoon held a four-storey building, 'Pavlov's House', for weeks.

On 19 November the Red Army, under plans by Georgy Zhukov and Aleksandr Vasilevsky, launched Operation Uranus, striking the weaker Romanian armies on the flanks; by late November it had encircled the 6th Army, with roughly 300,000 German and Axis troops. Relief efforts failed, Hitler forbade a breakout, and the trapped army starved through the winter. Paulus's army capitulated on 2 February 1943, the first of Hitler's field armies to surrender; nearly 100,000 were taken prisoner, most of whom died in Soviet camps. Axis losses are put between 800,000 and 1.5 million killed, wounded or captured. Germany never recovered the initiative in the east.

Q80034.title: Armenian genocide
Q80034.place: Ottoman Empire (Anatolia and the Syrian desert)
paras: The Armenian genocide was the systematic destruction of the Armenian people of the Ottoman Empire during the First World War. It was carried out by the ruling Committee of Union and Progress (the 'Young Turks'), led by Talaat Pasha and Enver Pasha, mainly through deportations and death marches from Anatolia into the Syrian desert, mass killings, and the forced conversion of others, chiefly women and children. About two million Armenians lived in the empire on the eve of the war.

Armenians, Christians in a Muslim empire, had long lived with lesser rights, and from the late 19th century the authorities came to see them as a threat; in the massacres of 1894 to 1896 under Sultan Abdul Hamid II at least 100,000 were killed. The Young Turks who seized power in 1908 turned to a radical Turkish nationalism and feared that the Armenian homeland in Anatolia would break away as the Balkans had. When the empire entered the war on Germany's side in 1914 and Enver's army was crushed by the Russians at Sarikamish in the winter of 1914-15, he blamed the Armenians for siding with Russia.

On the night of 23-24 April 1915 hundreds of Armenian intellectuals and community leaders were arrested in Constantinople, and most were later killed; Armenians mark 24 April as the beginning of the genocide. On Talaat's orders, an estimated 800,000 to 1.2 million Armenians were then driven on death marches to the Syrian desert in 1915 and 1916, without food or water. Men were often killed outright; a 'Special Organization' of irregulars, many of them released convicts, carried out massacres, children were taken and converted, and Muslim settlers took over Armenian homes and property.

By 1922 only about 388,000 Armenians remained in the empire. After the Ottoman defeat in 1918 the leaders fled to Germany; several, Talaat among them, were later assassinated by Armenian avengers. Together with the concurrent Assyrian and Greek genocides, the destruction of the Armenians helped make possible an ethnically Turkish state, the Republic of Turkey, whose government still denies that it was genocide. Almost all historians outside Turkey accept it as such, and 36 countries had recognised it by 2026, the United States in 2021.

Q8690.title: Cultural Revolution
paras: The Cultural Revolution (in full, the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution) was the political upheaval Mao Zedong, chairman of the Chinese Communist Party, launched in 1966 and which lasted until his death in 1976. Mao, whose standing had suffered after the disastrous Great Leap Forward and the famine that followed it, claimed that bourgeois elements had infiltrated the party and society to restore capitalism, and set out to purge his rivals and reassert his authority, with the help of radicals including his wife Jiang Qing and the defence minister Lin Biao.

In May 1966 the Politburo set up the Maoist Cultural Revolution Group, and in August Mao called on the young to take party leaders to task; schools were closed, and students formed paramilitary bands of Red Guards. They attacked teachers, intellectuals and officials and set out to destroy the 'Four Olds' (old customs, culture, habits and ideas), wrecking temples, artefacts and historic sites. A personality cult grew around Mao, and Lin Biao had the 'Little Red Book' of his quotations printed by the millions. Head of state Liu Shaoqi was purged and died in prison in 1969, and Deng Xiaoping was removed. As Red Guard factions fought one another and cities neared anarchy, Mao sent in the army from 1967 and more than ten million urban young people were sent to the countryside.

Lin Biao was named Mao's successor in 1969 but died in a plane crash in Mongolia in September 1971, apparently fleeing to the Soviet Union. Premier Zhou Enlai then restored some order and some purged officials, while the radical 'Gang of Four' around Jiang Qing gained influence. Deng, brought back in the 1970s, was purged again in April 1976; after Mao died that September, the Gang of Four were arrested.

Estimates of the dead range from about 1 to 2 million, and tens of millions were persecuted, imprisoned or humiliated; industrial output in 1968 fell 12 percent below that of 1966. Deng Xiaoping became paramount leader in 1978 and dismantled the ideology of the Cultural Revolution with the 'reform and opening up'.

Q49077.title: Six-Day War
Q49077.place: Sinai, the West Bank and Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights
paras: The Six-Day War of 5 to 10 June 1967 was fought between Israel and its Arab neighbours Egypt, Jordan and Syria, with support from Iraq. In six days Israel took the Sinai Peninsula and the Gaza Strip from Egypt, the West Bank and East Jerusalem from Jordan and the Golan Heights from Syria, reshaping the Middle East into the 21st century.

Tension had built since the wars of 1948 and 1956. Syrian-backed Palestinian guerrillas raided across the border and Israel struck back, and in April 1967 Israeli and Syrian forces fought an air battle. In May a Soviet report, which was false, told Egypt that Israel was massing troops against Syria. President Gamal Abdel Nasser moved his army into Sinai, expelled the United Nations Emergency Force that had guarded the border for more than a decade, and on 22 May closed the Straits of Tiran, Israel's only outlet to the Red Sea; at the end of May he signed a defence pact with King Hussein of Jordan. Israel's leaders decided to strike first.

On the morning of 5 June the Israeli air force launched Operation Focus: some 200 aircraft flew out low over the Mediterranean and hit Egypt's airfields from the north, destroying most of its air force on the ground, then struck Jordan, Syria and Iraq. Israeli armour and infantry drove into Sinai and Gaza; after Field Marshal Abdel Hakim Amer ordered a retreat, the Egyptian army was routed. Jordan opened fire in Jerusalem the same day, and on 7 June Israeli troops took the Old City and prayed at the Western Wall. On 9 and 10 June Israel stormed the Golan Heights. Egypt and Jordan accepted a ceasefire on 8 June and Syria on 10 June.

About 20,000 Arabs and some 800 Israelis were killed. Nasser resigned, only to return after mass demonstrations in his favour; at Khartoum in August the Arab states answered with 'no peace, no recognition, no negotiation' with Israel. Some 280,000 to 325,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from the West Bank and about 100,000 Syrians from the Golan. Israel returned Sinai to Egypt in 1982 and left Gaza in 2005, but the territories taken in 1967 remain at the centre of the Arab-Israeli conflict.

Q40949.title: American Revolutionary War
Q40949.place: The Thirteen Colonies of British North America
paras: The American Revolutionary War, from 1775 to 1783, was fought between Great Britain and thirteen of its North American colonies, which declared their independence in 1776 as the United States. France joined the Americans in 1778 and Spain allied itself with France in 1779, turning a colonial rebellion into a world war.

The quarrel grew out of the costly Seven Years' War, after which Parliament tried to raise revenue in the colonies with the Stamp Act of 1765, the Townshend Acts of 1767 and the Tea Act of 1773. Colonists protested against taxation without representation; British soldiers killed five men in the Boston Massacre of 1770, and in December 1773 Bostonians threw 342 chests of tea into the harbour. Parliament answered with the punitive 'Intolerable Acts', and a First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia in September 1774.

Fighting began on 19 April 1775, when British troops marching from Boston to seize arms at Concord clashed with militia at Lexington and Concord. The Second Continental Congress formed a Continental Army under George Washington, the British won a costly victory at Bunker Hill in June, and in March 1776 they evacuated Boston. On 4 July 1776 Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence. The British took New York, but in October 1777 John Burgoyne's army, marching down from Canada, surrendered at Saratoga; the victory persuaded France to enter the war openly.

After the hard winter at Valley Forge, where the Prussian officer Baron von Steuben drilled Washington's army, the war moved south: the British took Georgia and, in May 1780, Charleston, but Nathanael Greene's campaign wore down Lord Cornwallis, who fell back to Yorktown in Virginia. There Washington and the French general Rochambeau besieged him while a French fleet blocked the sea, and on 19 October 1781 Cornwallis surrendered his army. In the Treaty of Paris of 3 September 1783 Britain recognised the independence of the United States, and separate treaties ended its war with France and Spain.

Q37643.title: Gulf War
paras: The Gulf War was fought between Iraq and a coalition of 42 countries led by the United States after Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990. It ended with the liberation of Kuwait on 28 February 1991.

Iraq's long war with Iran had ended in a ceasefire in 1988. In July 1990 Saddam Hussein accused Kuwait of taking oil from the Rumaila fields on their border, demanded that Kuwait and Saudi Arabia write off some $30 billion of Iraqi debt, and massed troops on the border; talks brokered by Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak broke down within hours. The invasion was condemned by the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union and most of the Arab League. On 8 August the first American aircraft arrived in Saudi Arabia to guard it, the start of the build-up known as Operation Desert Shield. Iraq first set up a puppet 'Republic of Kuwait' and on 28 August annexed the whole country, calling it Iraq's 19th province.

On 29 November the UN Security Council authorised 'all necessary means' if Iraq did not leave Kuwait by 15 January 1991. By then the coalition had gathered some 750,000 troops, 540,000 of them American. Operation Desert Storm began on 17 January with a huge air campaign against Iraq's air defences, communications, weapons plants and oil refineries, using stealth aircraft, cruise missiles and laser-guided bombs; Iraq fired Scud missiles, some of them at Israel. The ground offensive opened on 24 February: coalition forces drove into Kuwait while American armour swung west into Iraq to strike the Republican Guard from behind. Retreating Iraqi troops set more than 600 Kuwaiti oil wells on fire. President George H. W. Bush declared a ceasefire on 28 February, after four days of ground fighting.

Iraq agreed to recognise Kuwait and give up its weapons of mass destruction. An estimated 8,000 to 10,000 Iraqi troops were killed, against about 300 coalition troops. Saddam Hussein stayed in power and crushed uprisings by Kurds in the north and Shia in the south; disputes over weapons inspections and the no-fly zones led on to the Iraq War of 2003.

Q11035.title: Telephone patented by Alexander Graham Bell
paras: On 7 March 1876 the United States Patent Office granted Alexander Graham Bell, a Scottish-born teacher of the deaf working in Boston, the patent for the electric telephone: a method of sending speech along a wire by electrical currents that varied in the same way as the vibrations of the air carrying the sound. It became the master patent from which the telephone industry grew.

Bell had come to the problem through his work on speech and hearing and his experiments with a 'harmonic telegraph' that would carry several telegraph messages on one wire. From 1875 he worked with the electrical mechanic Thomas Watson, and on 2 June 1875 an accidentally plucked reed showed him that a wire could carry the overtones needed for speech. Others were working on the same idea, among them Elisha Gray, who filed a caveat for a telephone design at the patent office on 14 February 1876, the same day as Bell's application, and Antonio Meucci, who had built a voice apparatus decades earlier.

Three days after the patent was granted, on 10 March 1876, Bell called Watson from another room of their Boston workshop with the words 'Mr. Watson, come here', the first successful call. His demonstration at the Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia that summer, where visitors included Emperor Pedro II of Brazil, brought the telephone international attention.

The Bell Telephone Company, later AT&T, was formed in 1877, and by 1886 more than 150,000 people in the United States had telephones. The patent was fought over for some twenty years: the Bell company faced some 550 legal challenges, including claims by Gray and Meucci and a move by the U.S. government in 1887 to annul the patent, and won them all. Who should be credited with the invention is still debated.

Q171328.title: Charter of the United Nations
paras: The Charter of the United Nations is the founding treaty of the United Nations. It was drafted at the United Nations Conference on International Organization in San Francisco, which opened on 25 April 1945, and signed there on 26 June 1945 by 50 of the 51 original member states.

The idea grew out of the Second World War. In August 1941 Franklin D. Roosevelt and Winston Churchill set out shared aims in the Atlantic Charter, and in January 1942 the Allies pledged themselves in the Declaration by United Nations, the basis of the later Charter. A new organisation to replace the failed League of Nations was first formally announced in the Moscow Declarations of 1943, and its outline was worked out by the great powers at talks hosted by the United States from August to October 1944.

The San Francisco conference was perhaps the largest international gathering held until then, with 850 delegates and some 3,500 participants in all. Each part of the text needed a two-thirds majority, and the final Charter was adopted unanimously. It set out the organisation's purposes of keeping peace and security, developing friendly relations among nations and cooperating on international problems, and created its main organs, including a General Assembly and a Security Council with power to investigate disputes and to authorise sanctions and the use of force, while forbidding the UN to intervene in matters essentially within a state's domestic jurisdiction.

The Charter came into force on 24 October 1945, once the five permanent members of the Security Council (the United States, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, France and China) and a majority of the other signatories had ratified it. That date, celebrated as United Nations Day, counts as the UN's birthday; the first General Assembly met in London in January 1946. Membership has since grown from 51 to 193 states.

Q10859.title: Spanish Civil War
paras: The Spanish Civil War, from July 1936 to April 1939, was fought between the Republicans, who defended the left-leaning Popular Front government of the Second Spanish Republic (socialists, communists, anarchists and Catalan and Basque autonomists, backed by the Soviet Union and Mexico), and the Nationalists, a rebellion of army officers joined by monarchists, Carlists, the fascist Falange and the Catholic right, backed by Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany. It ended with the dictatorship of General Francisco Franco.

The Republic had been proclaimed in 1931 when King Alfonso XIII went into exile. Its reforms divided the country: the Church, the landowners and much of the army opposed it, the right won the elections of 1933, and Franco put down a socialist rising in Asturias in 1934. When the Popular Front narrowly won the elections of February 1936, officers began plotting a coup, with General Emilio Mola as chief planner and the exiled General José Sanjurjo as its figurehead; Franco, sent away to the Canary Islands, joined late.

The rising began in Spanish Morocco on 17 July 1936 and spread to garrisons across the mainland the next day. The rebels took Morocco and the conservative heartland, but the Republic held about two-thirds of the country, including Madrid and most big cities, so the coup turned into a war. Sanjurjo died in a plane crash days later, and Franco, after ferrying his Army of Africa across the strait in German and Italian aircraft, became Nationalist commander-in-chief and head of state in October 1936. Both sides killed thousands of suspected opponents behind their lines. Madrid held out under siege from November 1936, helped by the foreign volunteers of the International Brigades, while the German Condor Legion gave the Nationalists command of the air; on 26 April 1937 it bombed the Basque town of Guernica. The Republicans were weakened by their own feuds, such as the street fighting in Barcelona in May 1937.

In 1938 the Nationalists drove through to the Mediterranean and cut the Republic in two; Barcelona fell in January 1939, and on 28 March Madrid surrendered. Franco declared victory on 1 April 1939. Hundreds of thousands of Republicans fled, mostly to camps in southern France, and many who stayed were persecuted. HISTORY.com puts the dead at up to a million, among them some 150,000 people killed by the Nationalists and about 49,000 by the Republicans away from the front. Franco ruled Spain until his death in 1975, and the war is often seen as a dress rehearsal for the Second World War.

Up to a million lives were lost; the Nationalists murdered about 150,000 prisoners and civilians and the Republicans about 49,000; Franco ruled until his death in 1975.
The war is seen as a dress rehearsal for WWII.

Q545449.title: Iraq War
paras: The Iraq War was fought in Iraq from 2003 to 2011. It began with an invasion by a coalition led by the United States, with the United Kingdom, Australia and Poland also sending combat troops, which overthrew the Ba'athist government of Saddam Hussein, and went on as a long insurgency against the occupying forces and the new Iraqi government.

The main case made for the war was that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction and that Saddam supported al-Qaeda; both claims proved false, and no such weapons were found. France, Germany and Russia urged continued diplomacy and weapons inspections, and the United States and its allies withdrew a draft UN resolution authorising force when it faced defeat. President George W. Bush gave Saddam 48 hours to leave Iraq, and some 90 minutes after the deadline passed, on 19 March 2003 in Washington (20 March in Iraq), cruise missiles struck the first targets in a 'shock and awe' bombing campaign.

Coalition forces quickly overwhelmed the Iraqi army; three weeks after the invasion began, Iraqis and U.S. soldiers pulled down Saddam's statue in Baghdad's Firdos Square, and on 1 May Bush declared the end of major combat. The occupation went badly. The Coalition Provisional Authority under L. Paul Bremer disbanded the Iraqi army and purged Ba'athists from the state, and the power vacuum fed an insurgency and a sectarian civil war between Iraq's Shia majority and Sunni minority, in which al-Qaeda in Iraq staged suicide bombings. Saddam was captured near Tikrit in December 2003, sentenced to death for crimes against humanity and hanged on 30 December 2006. Power passed to an Iraqi interim government in June 2004, and elections, a new constitution and a government under Nouri al-Maliki followed. The prisoner abuse at Abu Ghraib, revealed in 2004, damaged the coalition's standing.

In 2007 Bush sent more troops (the 'surge'), which helped stabilise parts of the country, and in 2008 he agreed to withdraw. Under President Barack Obama the combat mission ended in 2010 and the last U.S. troops left in December 2011. Nearly 4,500 Americans were killed; estimates of the total dead range from about 150,000 to over a million, including well over 100,000 Iraqi civilians. The war's aftermath helped give rise to the Islamic State, which drew the United States back into Iraq in 2014.

Q466.title: World Wide Web proposed at CERN
paras: In March 1989 Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist working at CERN, the European particle physics laboratory near Geneva, wrote the first proposal for what became the World Wide Web: a system linking documents on computers across a network by hypertext. CERN's research community of thousands of scientists, spread over universities and institutes in many countries, needed an easy way to share information, and the idea was to merge computers, data networks and hypertext into one simple global information system. Berners-Lee had already built a private hypertext system at CERN, ENQUIRE, in 1980.

The proposal, which did not yet name the system, was formalised with the Belgian engineer Robert Cailliau as a management proposal for a 'WorldWideWeb' hypertext project in November 1990. By the end of 1990 Berners-Lee had the first web server and browser working at CERN on a NeXT computer, which carried a hand-written label warning not to switch it off. In building it he defined the first versions of the three foundations of the Web: the HTTP protocol, the URL address and the HTML page format. The first website was at info.cern.ch.

The software was released to other research institutions from early 1991 and announced to the whole Internet in August 1991; the first web server in the United States came online at SLAC, the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center, in December 1991. On 30 April 1993 CERN put the Web's code in the public domain royalty-free. The same year the Mosaic browser, from the NCSA at the University of Illinois, made the Web easy to use on ordinary PCs and Macintoshes, and its growth exploded: by the end of 1994 there were some 10,000 web servers and 10 million users. Berners-Lee left CERN in 1994 for MIT, where he founded the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) to keep the Web an open standard.

Q33761.title: Arab Spring
Q33761.place: North Africa and the Middle East
paras: The Arab Spring was a wave of loosely connected pro-democracy protests and uprisings that spread across the Arab world from Tunisia at the end of 2010 into 2011 and 2012. It brought down the rulers of Tunisia, Egypt, Libya and Yemen, but in several countries it turned into civil war or a return to authoritarian rule.

It began on 17 December 2010, when Mohamed Bouazizi, a street vendor in Tunisia whose vegetable stall had been seized by police, set himself on fire in protest. Demonstrations spread across the country, and on 14 January 2011 President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, who had ruled for more than twenty years, fled to Saudi Arabia. Behind the anger lay corruption, unemployment, poverty and a large population of educated young people without prospects, and protesters used social media to get round state-controlled news.

The example spread fast. Mass protests filled Tahrir Square in Cairo from 25 January, and on 11 February Egypt's Hosni Mubarak stepped down. Uprisings followed in Libya, Yemen, Syria (from 15 March) and Bahrain, and sustained demonstrations in Morocco, Algeria, Iraq, Jordan and elsewhere. In Libya the revolt became a civil war, and Muammar Gaddafi was captured and killed by rebels on 20 October 2011; Yemen's Ali Abdullah Saleh signed a power-sharing deal in November and left office in February 2012. In Bahrain the protests were crushed with help from neighbouring states.

Only Tunisia, which held its first democratic elections in October 2011, kept a lasting democratic opening. In Egypt the elected president Mohamed Morsi was overthrown in a military coup in 2013 that brought Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to power; Syria, Libya and Yemen sank into long civil wars, in which the Islamic State seized territory, and millions fled as refugees. The turmoil that followed is sometimes called the Arab Winter; a new wave of protests from 2018 toppled the rulers of Sudan and Algeria in 2019.

vprinting-press.title: Gutenberg's movable-type printing press
paras: By about 1450 Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith from a patrician family of Mainz on the Rhine, had a working printing press with movable metal type in operation in his home city, then part of the Holy Roman Empire. Printing from carved blocks and even movable type, first made of baked clay by Bi Sheng in 11th-century China, was long known in East Asia, but Gutenberg's combination of techniques made printing fast and cheap enough to transform Europe.

He had begun experimenting in Strasbourg, where he lived in exile from Mainz in the 1430s, and returned to Mainz in the 1440s. His system brought several inventions together: individual letters cast in large numbers in a hand mould from an alloy of lead, tin and antimony; an oil-based ink that stuck to metal; and a wooden screw press adapted from the presses used for wine and olives. To pay for the work he borrowed 800 guilders, and then another 800, from the Mainz moneylender Johann Fust, and Peter Schöffer, a former scribe, joined the business.

The press printed indulgences for the Church and smaller works, and its great project, begun in 1452, was the Bible in Latin with 42 lines to a column. Around 1455 some 180 copies were finished, most on paper and the rest on vellum; the future Pope Pius II, who saw pages in Frankfurt, praised how clear and easy to read the type was. In 1455 Fust sued Gutenberg for his money, and the equipment passed to Fust and Schöffer, who carried on printing. Gutenberg died in 1468.

Printing spread fast, carried by men who had worked with Gutenberg: to Italy by 1465 and to England with William Caxton in 1476. By the end of the 15th century some 270 European cities had presses, which had produced over 20 million copies by 1500. The flood of cheap books spread ideas across Europe as never before and helped bring about the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution.

cp02-07.title: Death of Muhammad; Abu Bakr becomes caliph
paras: The Prophet Muhammad died in Medina on 8 June 632, ten years after his migration there from Mecca and soon after his followers had brought Mecca and much of Arabia under their rule. He left no agreed successor, and in the hours after his death the leaders of the community chose his close companion and father-in-law Abu Bakr to lead it, the first of the caliphs ('successors').

The community was stunned. Umar, one of the leading companions, at first refused to believe that Muhammad was dead and threatened anyone who said so. Abu Bakr, after seeing the body, addressed the people at the mosque: whoever worshipped Muhammad should know that Muhammad was dead, but whoever worshipped God should know that God lives and does not die.

Meanwhile the Ansar, the Muslims native to Medina, gathered in the courtyard (saqifa) of the Banu Sa'ida clan, apparently to choose a leader of their own. Abu Bakr and Umar hurried there. Abu Bakr argued that only a man of Muhammad's tribe, the Quraysh, would be accepted by the Arabs; when one of the Ansar proposed two leaders, one from each group, the meeting grew heated, and Umar took Abu Bakr's hand and swore allegiance to him, followed by the others. The choice was not unanimous: several companions, above all Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law Ali, held back their allegiance at first; Ali made peace with Abu Bakr only after six months.

Abu Bakr ruled for only about two years, until his death in 634. He put down the revolts of Arab tribes and rival prophets such as Musaylima in the Ridda ('apostasy') Wars, uniting the whole Arabian Peninsula under Medina, and sent Khalid ibn al-Walid against the Sasanian and Byzantine empires, opening the great Arab conquests continued by his successor Umar. The dispute over who should have succeeded Muhammad lies at the root of the division between Sunni Muslims, who honour Abu Bakr as the first rightly guided caliph, and Shia Muslims, who hold that leadership belonged to Ali.
